title: Deploy Backend (Microservices, Workers & RAG Chatbot)
content:
In this section, we will package and deploy all 12 AWS Lambda Backend functions (5 REST API Microservices, 3 Event-Driven Workers, and 4 RAG Chatbot Lambdas) onto the AWS infrastructure provisioned via Terraform, and configure secret keys in AWS Secrets Manager.
Prerequisites Python 3.12, pip, and AWS CLI v2 installed and configured (aws configure). Cloned project repository: https://github.com/lointt/phutungxemay-platform. Open Terminal / PowerShell and navigate to the project root: cd <project-path>/phutungxemay-platform Set the environment suffix variable (default Lab if following Section 5.2): # Windows PowerShell $ENV_TITLE = "Lab" # macOS / Linux export ENV_TITLE="Lab" Step 1: Update Secrets in AWS Secrets Manager Before testing the backend, populate the Google Gemini API Key (and VNPay / GHN / SMTP credentials if applicable) in Secrets Manager:
Open AWS Console -> Navigate to Secrets Manager (ap-southeast-1). Select chatbot/gemini_api_key_lab -> Click Retrieve secret value -> Edit. Replace GEMINI_API_KEY with the real API Key from Google AI Studio -> Click Save. (Optional) Review or update the remaining secrets: ecommerce/vnpay_lab (VNPAY_TMN_CODE, VNPAY_HASH_SECRET) ecommerce/shipping_api_key_lab (SHIPPING_API_KEY - GHN Token) ecommerce/smtp_password_lab (SMTP_PASSWORD - Gmail App Password) Step 2: Package & Deploy 5 REST API Microservices The 5 core services (catalog, cart, order, payment_webhook, user) rely solely on Python standard libraries and boto3 (built into AWS Lambda Runtime), so we package handler.py directly as lambda_function.py:
On Windows (PowerShell):
$services = @( @{ dir="backend/services/catalog"; fn="CatalogServiceHandler-$ENV_TITLE" }, @{ dir="backend/services/cart"; fn="CartServiceHandler-$ENV_TITLE" }, @{ dir="backend/services/order"; fn="OrderServiceHandler-$ENV_TITLE" }, @{ dir="backend/services/payment_webhook"; fn="PaymentWebhookHandler-$ENV_TITLE" }, @{ dir="backend/services/user"; fn="UserProfileHandler-$ENV_TITLE" } ) foreach ($s in $services) { python -c "import zipfile; z=zipfile.ZipFile('pkg.zip','w'); z.write('$($s.dir)/handler.py','lambda_function.py'); z.close()" aws lambda update-function-code --function-name $s.fn --zip-file fileb://pkg.zip Remove-Item pkg.zip -Force } On macOS / Linux (Bash):
for item in "catalog:CatalogServiceHandler" "cart:CartServiceHandler" "order:OrderServiceHandler" "payment_webhook:PaymentWebhookHandler" "user:UserProfileHandler"; do dir="${item%%:*}" fn="${item##*:}-${ENV_TITLE}" python3 -c "import zipfile; z=zipfile.ZipFile('pkg.zip','w'); z.write('backend/services/${dir}/handler.py','lambda_function.py'); z.close()" aws lambda update-function-code --function-name "$fn" --zip-file fileb://pkg.zip rm -f pkg.zip done Expected Result:
Step 3: Package & Deploy 3 Event-Driven Workers Deploy the 3 background workers (InventoryWorker, ShippingWorker, NotificationWorker):
On Windows (PowerShell): $workers = @( @{ dir="backend/workers/inventory"; fn="InventoryWorker-$ENV_TITLE" }, @{ dir="backend/workers/shipping"; fn="ShippingWorker-$ENV_TITLE" }, @{ dir="backend/workers/notification"; fn="NotificationWorker-$ENV_TITLE" } ) foreach ($w in $workers) { python -c "import zipfile; z=zipfile.ZipFile('pkg.zip','w'); z.write('$($w.dir)/handler.py','lambda_function.py'); z.close()" aws lambda update-function-code --function-name $w.fn --zip-file fileb://pkg.zip Remove-Item pkg.zip -Force } Expected Result:
Step 4: Package & Deploy RAG Chatbot Cluster (4 Lambdas) The Chatbot cluster requires bundling Linux x86_64 compatible dependencies (PyJWT, cryptography for the Authorizer, and google-genai for Orchestrator & Sync-to-KB).
4.1. Deploy ChatReceiverHandler (Zero external dependencies) python -c "import zipfile; z=zipfile.ZipFile('receiver.zip','w'); z.write('backend/services/chatbot_receiver/handler.py','lambda_function.py'); z.close()" aws lambda update-function-code --function-name "ChatReceiverHandler-$ENV_TITLE" --zip-file fileb://receiver.zip Remove-Item receiver.zip -Force Expected Result:
4.2. Deploy ChatAuthorizerHandler (With PyJWT & cryptography) mkdir -Force build_auth pip install PyJWT cryptography -t build_auth --platform manylinux2014_x86_64 --only-binary=:all: --python-version 3.12 Copy-Item backend/services/chatbot_authorizer/handler.py build_auth/lambda_function.py Compress-Archive -Path "build_auth\*" -DestinationPath "authorizer.zip" -Force aws lambda update-function-code --function-name "ChatAuthorizerHandler-$ENV_TITLE" --zip-file fileb://authorizer.zip Remove-Item -Recurse -Force build_auth, authorizer.zip Expected Result:
4.3. Deploy ChatOrchestratorHandler & DynamoDBSyncToKBHandler (With google-genai) mkdir -Force build_genai pip install google-genai -t build_genai --platform manylinux2014_x86_64 --only-binary=:all: --python-version 3.12 # 1. ChatOrchestratorHandler Copy-Item backend/services/chatbot_orchestrator/handler.py build_genai/lambda_function.py -Force Compress-Archive -Path "build_genai\*" -DestinationPath "orchestrator.zip" -Force aws lambda update-function-code --function-name "ChatOrchestratorHandler-$ENV_TITLE" --zip-file fileb://orchestrator.zip # 2. DynamoDBSyncToKBHandler Copy-Item backend/services/sync_to_kb/handler.py build_genai/lambda_function.py -Force Compress-Archive -Path "build_genai\*" -DestinationPath "sync_to_kb.zip" -Force aws lambda update-function-code --function-name "DynamoDBSyncToKBHandler-$ENV_TITLE" --zip-file fileb://sync_to_kb.zip Remove-Item -Recurse -Force build_genai, orchestrator.zip, sync_to_kb.zip Expected Result:
Step 5: Verify Deployment Status Open AWS Console -> Lambda -> Functions and filter by -Lab (or the environment suffix). Confirm all 13 Lambda functions (1 SSR + 12 Backend) show recent Last modified timestamps and Active status.

title: Deploy Frontend (Next.js SSR)
content:
In this section, we will download the Frontend (Next.js) source code from GitHub, configure it to connect with the AWS infrastructure provisioned via Terraform, test it Locally, and deploy it to AWS (S3 + Lambda SSR + CloudFront) using OpenNext.
Environment Prerequisites Before starting, ensure we have completed provisioning the AWS infrastructure with Terraform in 5.2-Prerequiste. Install Node.js version 20 or higher (Recommended: Node.js 22 LTS) from nodejs.org. Verify the Node.js installation in Terminal / PowerShell:
node -v npm -v Step 1: Clone the Frontend Source Code The Frontend source code is located in the frontend directory on GitHub: https://github.com/lointt/phutungxemay-platform/tree/main/frontend.
Option 1: Clone the entire repository (if not cloned during the Terraform step)
git clone https://github.com/lointt/phutungxemay-platform.git cd phutungxemay-platform/frontend Option 2: Already cloned the repository Simply navigate into the frontend directory:
cd <project-path>/phutungxemay-platform/frontend Step 2: Install Dependencies Run the following command inside the frontend folder to install all required packages (Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, Cognito SDK, OpenNext):
npm ci (Alternatively, we can run npm install.)
Step 3: Configure Environment Variables (.env.local) Create a file named .env.local inside the frontend/ folder and populate it with the values from the Terraform Outputs:
NEXT_PUBLIC_CDN_BASE_URL=https://<cloudfront_domain_name> NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL=https://<cloudfront_domain_name> NEXT_PUBLIC_COGNITO_USER_POOL_ID=<cognito_user_pool_id> NEXT_PUBLIC_COGNITO_CLIENT_ID=<cognito_client_id> NEXT_PUBLIC_WEBSOCKET_URL=<chatbot_websocket_url> Step 4: Run TypeScript Check and Local Testing Verify TypeScript code validity:
npx tsc --noEmit (No output means the codebase has zero TypeScript errors.)
Start the local development server:
npm run dev Open the browser and navigate to: http://localhost:3000
Verify the homepage layout, product catalog, login/register flow, and the AI Chatbot widget at the bottom-right corner. Once verified, press Ctrl + C in the Terminal to stop the local server. Expected Result:
Step 5: Build and Deploy Frontend to AWS (OpenNext + S3 + Lambda + CloudFront) To run the website completely Serverless on AWS, we use OpenNext to bundle Next.js into two parts: Static Assets (uploaded to S3) and SSR Server Function (deployed to AWS Lambda).
5.1. Build the Application with OpenNext npm run build:open-next Once completed, the .open-next/ directory will be generated containing the optimized build artifacts.
Expected Result:
5.2. Sync Static Assets to S3 Hosting Bucket Replace <s3_hosting_bucket_name> with the bucket name from Terraform Outputs (e.g., phutungxemay-frontend-lab-2026):
aws s3 sync .open-next/assets s3://<s3_hosting_bucket_name> --delete Expected Result:
5.3. Sync Product Images to S3 Images Bucket Replace <s3_product_images_bucket_name> with the product images bucket name (e.g., phutungxemay-product-images-lab-2026):
aws s3 sync public/images s3://<s3_product_images_bucket_name>/images --cache-control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable" Expected Result:
5.4. Package and Update the Next.js SSR Lambda Function On Windows (PowerShell): Compress-Archive -Path ".open-next\server-functions\default\*" -DestinationPath "function.zip" -Force aws lambda update-function-code --function-name <lambda_nextjs_function_name> --zip-file fileb://function.zip On macOS / Linux (Bash): cd .open-next/server-functions/default zip -rq ../../../../function.zip . cd ../../../.. aws lambda update-function-code --function-name <lambda_nextjs_function_name> --zip-file fileb://function.zip (Replace <lambda_nextjs_function_name> with the Lambda function name from Outputs, e.g., NextjsServerHandler-Lab.) Expected Result:
5.5. Invalidate CloudFront Cache Replace <cloudfront_distribution_id> with the CloudFront distribution ID from Outputs:
aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id <cloudfront_distribution_id> --paths "/*" Expected Result:
Step 6: Verify Deployment Wait approximately 30 – 60 seconds for CloudFront to propagate the cache invalidation. Open the browser and navigate directly to https://<cloudfront_domain_name>. The Serverless Motorcycle E-Commerce website and AI Chatbot are now live on AWS! Expected Result:

title: Introduction
content:
Workshop Overview This workshop builds a Serverless E-Commerce Website integrated with a Full-Duplex AI RAG Chatbot on AWS, deployed in the ap-southeast-1 (Singapore) region. The architecture consists of two primary execution flows alongside dedicated Security and Monitoring layers.
Flow 1: Serverless E-Commerce Website CDN: Users access the website through Amazon CloudFront, protected at the edge by Edge WAF (CloudFront Function). Frontend Delivery: CloudFront distributes Product Images (S3), Frontend Assets (S3), and Frontend SSR Service (Lambda). Authentication: Amazon Cognito handles user registration, sign-in, and password recovery. REST API Gateway: Business API requests pass through Amazon API Gateway (REST API). Business Logic Lambdas: User Profile (customer details), Catalog (products), Cart (shopping cart), Order (order placement), and Payment Webhook (online payment via VNPay Sandbox). Data Persistence: Application data is stored in Amazon DynamoDB. Event-Driven Processing: Amazon EventBridge receives domain events such as OrderPlaced and PaymentSuccess, routing them to three SQS + Lambda worker pairs: Inventory Queue + Inventory Worker: deducts product stock. Notification Queue + Notification Worker: sends email notifications via Gmail SMTP. Shipping Queue + Shipping Worker: creates shipping orders with GHN Sandbox. Change Data Capture (CDC): DynamoDB Streams captures real-time data modifications in DynamoDB. Knowledge Synchronization: The DynamoDB Sync to S3 Lambda uses the Google Gemini API to generate embeddings and stores them in the Vector Knowledge Base (S3). Flow 2: Full-Duplex RAG Chatbot WebSocket API Gateway: Users connect to Amazon API Gateway (WebSocket API) for real-time two-way chat. Session Authorization: The Chat Authorizer Lambda authenticates sessions for both guest visitors and logged-in customers via Cognito. Message Ingestion: The Chat Receiver Lambda receives incoming frames and asynchronously dispatches them to Chat Orchestrator, preventing the 29-second WebSocket timeout limit. Chat Orchestrator: Persists chat sessions to DynamoDB, retrieves embeddings from the Vector Knowledge Base (S3), and uses Gemini 2.0 Flash to answer customer inquiries. When a customer requests human assistance, the Lambda publishes a HumanRequested event to EventBridge. Security Group AWS IAM: Manages access permissions following the principle of least privilege. IAM Access Analyzer: Detects unintended public access and overly permissive policies. AWS Secrets Manager: Securely stores secrets including API keys, VNPay, GHN, and SMTP credentials. AWS KMS: Manages cryptographic keys for data encryption. Monitoring Group AWS Budgets: Tracks monthly cloud spending thresholds. AWS CloudTrail: Audits account activity via Event History. Amazon CloudWatch Logs: Captures runtime logs and errors from Lambda functions. Amazon CloudWatch Alarms: Triggers alerts when metrics breach thresholds or errors occur. Amazon SNS: Delivers CloudWatch Alarm notifications to Gmail.

title: Event 1
content:
Summary Report: “The Thinking Behind Building The Bot” Event Information Time: Saturday, 26/09/2026, 09:00 – 12:00 Location: 26F, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City Participation Role: Attendee Organizers: CMC Global in cooperation with AWS First Cloud Journey Format: In-person talkshow, combined with a Buildathon kickoff and a mock interview session Event Objectives Show that building an enterprise bot takes far more than calling an LLM API Explain the design mindset behind reliable bots: architecture, context handling, latency, cost and data protection Present how to deploy bots on AWS with Amazon Bedrock and serverless services Give participants practical career advice through mock interviews Speakers Bui Nhat Truong – Technical Leader, CMC Global Agenda Time Activity Details 09:00 – 09:30 Buildathon Kickoff Launch of the technical challenge series, explanation of the rules and evaluation criteria, and team networking 09:30 – 11:15 Talkshow: The Thinking Behind Building The Bot System design, data flow, RAG architecture and LLM orchestration on AWS 11:15 – 12:00 Mock Interview and Career Coaching Live mock interviews for Cloud/AI roles, feedback on answers and open Q&A Key Highlights Enterprise-grade bot mindset A bot for business use differs greatly from a chat window where someone types a prompt:
Context management: keep only the useful parts of the conversation history, which lowers token cost and avoids overflowing the context window RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): ground answers in the company’s own data through embedding models and a vector database Guardrails and safety: filter harmful input, defend against prompt injection and keep answers within company policy Deploying on AWS Amazon Bedrock and Knowledge Bases: access several foundation models through one standard API, with RAG built in Serverless compute: AWS Lambda and Amazon API Gateway handle event-driven webhooks and cost almost nothing while idle Credential security: store API keys and secrets in AWS Secrets Manager rather than hardcoding them in source code Quote from the speaker A great AI assistant is not decided by having the biggest model, but by sound architecture: how latency is controlled, how accurate the information is, and how well the system recovers from unexpected cases.
Mock interview session Interviewer’s view: Tech Leads and Solution Architects value problem-solving ability, honesty about what you know and the ability to learn on your own, more than memorized syntax STAR method: describe lab work and projects as Situation → Task → Action → Result Networking: a chance to talk directly with engineers from CMC Global and AWS Key Takeaways Design Mindset Before this talk, I mostly thought about which model to choose. Now I would start with what the bot must do and what can go wrong Latency, cost and accuracy pull against each other, so they need to be discussed before building, not after Technical Architecture RAG, context control and guardrails each solve a different problem, and a reliable bot needs all three Managed AWS services (Bedrock, Lambda, API Gateway, Secrets Manager) leave more time for the logic of the bot itself A secret that reaches a repository should be treated as already exposed Career Mindset Saying clearly what I do not know is better than guessing A small project explained well with STAR can say more than a long list of tools Applying to Work Design project chatbots with RAG and selective context management instead of sending the whole history to the model Add guardrails such as input filtering and prompt-injection checks to any bot I build Try Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases for a small question-answering prototype Use Lambda and API Gateway for lightweight bot backends Move credentials to AWS Secrets Manager in my projects Practice STAR answers based on my AWS labs and course projects Event Experience I came to “The Thinking Behind Building The Bot” expecting to hear mainly about models and prompts. What stayed with me instead was how much careful work happens around the model.
Learning from the speaker The speaker kept returning to architecture, which made me look at chatbots from the system side rather than the prompt side. The parts on context management and RAG explained why a bot can sound confident and still be wrong. Technical exposure Seeing Bedrock, Lambda, API Gateway and Secrets Manager placed in one picture helped me connect services I had been learning separately. Mock interview and career guidance Watching the mock interviews made me realize that how a candidate reasons matters more than a perfect answer. STAR gave me a simple order to follow when I talk about my labs and projects. Networking and discussions Talking with engineers from CMC Global and AWS mentors gave me a clearer idea of how cloud and information security meet in real work. Lessons learned A bot should be judged by how it behaves in difficult cases, not only by a good demo. As an Information Assurance student, I should ask early what data the bot can reach and who can reach it. I need to practice explaining my work simply, because good technical work still has to be understood by others. Some event photos I left the talkshow with a different first question: not “which model should I use?”, but “what does this system need to be trusted?”

title: Blog 1
content:
AMAZON INSPECTOR – HOW DOES AWS AUTOMATICALLY SCAN VULNERABILITIES FOR YOUR SYSTEM? Link to the original post: AWS Study Group VN – Facebook
Security is often thought of mainly as configuring IAM permissions and closing unnecessary ports. However, a server can be well-configured and still be compromised simply because the software inside remains unpatched. A single outdated library or an unpatched OS package is enough to give attackers a way in.
1. WHAT IS AMAZON INSPECTOR? Simply put, it is AWS’s automated vulnerability management service. Once enabled, it automatically discovers your running workloads and scans them for software vulnerabilities as well as unintended network exposure to the Internet. You do not need to schedule scans or trigger them manually.
2. HOW DOES IT WORK? It operates in 3 main steps:
Input Data (Resource Discovery): Inspector automatically discovers what needs to be scanned: EC2 instances (using SSM Agent or agentless scanning), container images in Amazon ECR, AWS Lambda functions, and source code in code repositories. You only need to enable the service without registering each resource manually. Analysis & Evaluation: Inspector correlates running software against the CVE database (publicly disclosed vulnerabilities). Whenever a new CVE is published, it automatically rescans your environment—meaning a system that was “clean” yesterday is not guaranteed to be clean today. In addition, it evaluates whether the resource is reachable from the Internet (Network Reachability) and whether the vulnerability is actively exploitable in the wild (Exploitability). Based on these factors, each finding is assigned a contextual Inspector Risk Score. Findings & Automated Response: Findings are aggregated in the Inspector console and pushed to AWS Security Hub for centralized visibility. Findings are also routed through Amazon EventBridge, allowing you to build automated remediation workflows—for example, invoking AWS Lambda to create support tickets, triggering SSM Patch Manager to apply patches, or sending alerts via Amazon SNS. Note that Inspector detects and reports vulnerabilities, while automated patching is an additional workflow you integrate. For the exact same vulnerability, if it resides on an Internet-facing server, its score will be significantly higher than on an internal-only instance. This helps teams prioritize what to patch first instead of staring at a list of hundreds of CVEs without knowing where to start.
3. PRICING & TARGET AUDIENCE Pricing: Inspector uses pay-as-you-go pricing based on usage, with no upfront commitment or minimum fee. New accounts receive a 15-day free trial for each scan type, allowing you to enable it, assess how many vulnerabilities exist in your environment, and estimate monthly costs. Note that CIS Benchmark assessments are excluded from the free trial. Detailed pricing varies by AWS Region and can be checked on the official AWS pricing page.
Who is it for? It is ideal for small and medium-sized businesses without a dedicated security team, or modern cloud architectures running containers, Lambda functions, and frequently updated third-party libraries—environments where tracking vulnerabilities manually is nearly impossible.
4. CONCLUSION The true value of Amazon Inspector does not lie in merely listing vulnerabilities—many tools can do that. What sets it apart is contextual risk scoring based on your system’s real-world exposure, helping you know exactly what to remediate first. Combined with Amazon EventBridge, the entire pipeline from detection and notification to remediation can run almost completely automatically.

Role-Based Access: Grouping users and using IAM Roles for services is much safer and easier to maintain than attaching policies to individual users. Verify Stock Deduction (InventoryWorker):

title: Prerequisites
content:
In this section, we will install Terraform and AWS CLI on the terminal, create Access Keys (Security Credentials) following the principle of least privilege, and provision the entire AWS Serverless infrastructure via Terraform IaC.
Part 1: Install Terraform and AWS CLI 1. Install Terraform (Recommended Version >= 1.9.0) Windows:
Option 1 (Recommended - Windows Package Manager): Open PowerShell (Run as Administrator) and run: winget install HashiCorp.Terraform Option 2 (Direct Download): Visit Terraform Downloads. title: Proposal
content:
Motorcycle E-Commerce & RAG Chatbot Platform A Serverless Motorcycle Parts Store and Intelligent Advisory Chatbot on AWS 1. Problem Overview This project addresses the challenge of advising on and retailing motorcycle parts online. The hardest part of this industry is the sheer number of part codes and motorcycle models, which makes it very easy for customers to buy the wrong part, while stores spend a lot of staff time answering chats. The system combines a Next.js e-commerce website with a RAG Chatbot (real-time part compatibility advice over WebSocket) on a 100% AWS Serverless platform. The solution automates consulting, processes orders asynchronously, provides strong security, and keeps operating costs extremely low.
2. Objectives & Scope Project Objectives
Consultation Automation: Build a real-time RAG AI virtual assistant to verify motorcycle spare parts compatibility across specific vehicle models and production years (response latency < 2s). Cost Optimization & Scalability: Leverage a 100% Serverless architecture on AWS, completely eliminating EC2 server maintenance overhead while maintaining operational costs below $6 USD/month. Asynchronous Business Processing: Apply Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) to decouple order checkout, inventory deduction, shipping fulfillment, and email notifications. Project Scope
In-Scope: Next.js 14 SSR e-commerce web application and 5 backend Lambda microservices. Customer authentication and administrative Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) via Amazon Cognito JWT. RAG AI Chatbot cluster via WebSocket API Gateway (integrated with S3 Vector Store and Google Gemini 2.0 Flash) alongside an on-duty staff escalation mechanism (Human Handover). Integration with VNPay Sandbox online payment gateway and Giao Hàng Nhanh (GHN) Sandbox logistics fulfillment. Event-driven orchestration utilizing Amazon EventBridge, 3 SQS queues equipped with Dead Letter Queues (DLQ), and 3 background workers (Inventory, Shipping, Notification). Comprehensive Infrastructure as Code (IaC) automation via Terraform and GitHub Actions CI/CD pipelines. Out-of-Scope: Physical retail Point-of-Sale (POS) systems for offline brick-and-mortar stores and direct international credit card payment processing (Stripe/PayPal). 3. Problem Statement Current problems
Customers without technical knowledge often order the wrong components/parts (wrong motorcycle model, wrong spark plug size, wrong chain and sprockets, etc.), leading to a high return rate. Staff spend a lot of time repeatedly answering the same questions: does this part fit my bike, is it in stock, how much does it cost. Renting fixed servers (EC2/VPS) incurs monthly maintenance costs even though traffic is uneven between day and night. Solution
Build the online store with Next.js 14 SSR and 5 Lambda microservices (Catalog, Cart, Order, User, Payment) behind API Gateway. Integrate an AI RAG Chatbot through API Gateway WebSocket: it automatically searches for compatible parts in a vector store kept on S3 and answers customers immediately. For difficult cases or complaints, the bot automatically forwards the information (Human Requested) to staff by email. Apply an event-driven architecture (EDA): EventBridge and SQS decouple inventory deduction, shipping order creation, and confirmation emails, with a DLQ to prevent the system from clogging. Secure online payment through the VNPay gateway with HMAC-SHA512 digital signature verification. Benefits and return on investment (ROI)
Reduces by more than 60% the time staff spend on chat duty answering basic questions. Reduces the wrong-part purchase rate to below 5%, since the bot verifies the correct motorcycle model before the customer orders. Extremely low infrastructure cost thanks to the serverless architecture and the pay-as-you-go model. The expected payback period is 3–6 months. 4. Solution Architecture The whole system runs on a Serverless model with no physical servers to manage. Users access the website through the CloudFront CDN; APIs are called through API Gateway REST; real-time chat goes through WebSocket; background tasks are pushed into EventBridge and SQS.
AWS services used
Amazon CloudFront & Functions: CDN for delivering the website, injecting security headers, and acting as an Edge WAF that blocks XSS, SQLi, etc. AWS Lambda: 13 functions: Next.js SSR, 5 backend microservices (Catalog, Cart, Order, User, Payment), the RAG Chatbot cluster (Chat Authorizer, Chat Receiver, Chat Orchestrator, DynamoDB Sync To S3), and 3 background workers (Inventory, Shipping, Notification). Amazon API Gateway: Provides the REST API for the website and the WebSocket API for the real-time chatbot. Amazon DynamoDB: Stores 6 data tables (Products, Orders, Carts, Users, StorePolicies, ChatbotSessions); Streams are enabled to automatically sync data to the AI knowledge base, and PITR backup is enabled. Amazon S3: Stores static website files, product images, and the Chatbot’s vector knowledge files. Amazon EventBridge & SQS: Orchestrates order events and message queues, including a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ). Amazon Cognito: Manages registration, sign-in, and customer/admin authorization using JWT. Amazon CloudWatch & SNS: System monitoring and error alerts via email. Amazon CloudTrail: Audit trail of edits/changes. AWS Secrets Manager: Securely stores secret keys. Component design
Frontend: S3 (images, static files) and a Next.js SSR Lambda for fast loading, supporting part search and filtering by motorcycle brand (Honda, Yamaha, etc.). Backend Microservices: Handle adding to cart, placing orders, updating accounts, and the VNPay payment webhook. RAG Chatbot: Receives messages over WebSocket and matches vectors on S3 to generate accurate advisory answers. Event Workers: Lambda InventoryWorker (deducts stock), ShippingWorker (creates GHN shipping orders), NotificationWorker (sends Gmail to customers/staff). 5. Technical Implementation Implementation phases
Architecture design & Terraform: design the serverless architecture in draw.io and write IaC code to automate the entire AWS infrastructure (2 weeks). Core Web & Microservices development: write 5 backend Lambdas in Python 3.12, build the Next.js frontend, and integrate VNPay sandbox payment (2 weeks). AI RAG & event-driven integration: set up the WebSocket channel, connect EventBridge to SQS, write the background worker Lambdas, and integrate GHN sandbox shipping (2 weeks). Security, testing & go-live: fix security vulnerabilities, set up CloudWatch Alarms, and run tests (2 weeks). Technical requirements
Use Terraform to manage infrastructure consistently and make it easy to redeploy when needed. Backend written in lightweight Python 3.12 with fast startup (low cold start). Apply Zero-Trust principles: verify permissions from the Cognito token, encrypt data at rest (SSE) and in transit (HTTPS/TLS). 6. Roadmap & Milestones Weeks 1–2: Finalize the architecture and complete the base infrastructure with Terraform. Weeks 3–4: Complete the backend microservices, the shopping website, and VNPay sandbox payment. Weeks 5–6: Complete the advisory RAG chatbot, the staff handover mechanism, the SQS event queues, and GHN sandbox shipping integration. Weeks 7–8: Security testing, cost optimization, and production launch. 7. Budget Estimation Costs can be viewed on the AWS Pricing Calculator Or see the budget estimate file.
Infrastructure costs (detailed estimate from the AWS spreadsheet for a scale of 1,000 users/month):
AWS Secrets Manager: USD 1.65/month (securely manages 4 secrets: Gemini Key, VNPay, GHN, Gmail SMTP; 10,000 API calls). Amazon CloudFront: USD 1.32/month (10 GB data transfer out, 50,000 HTTPS requests, and the Edge WAF filter). Amazon CloudWatch: USD 1.30/month (1 GB log data ingested, 6 metric alarms, and 1 monitoring dashboard). Amazon DynamoDB: USD 0.52/month (USD 0.29 for on-demand read/write capacity and USD 0.23 for PITR backup protecting 1 GB of data; Streams are free at USD 0). Amazon API Gateway: USD 0.23/month (50,000 REST API requests and 20,000 WebSocket messages). S3 Standard: USD 0.09/month (3 GB of image & vector storage, 1,000 PUT requests, and 15,000 GET requests). AWS Key Management Service (KMS): USD 0.03/month (10,000 symmetric requests for encrypting secret keys). AWS Lambda: USD 0.00/month (500,000 requests, 512 MB memory, fully within the 1 million requests Free Tier allowance). Amazon Cognito: USD 0.00/month (1,000 monthly active users (MAU), free within the 50,000 MAU Free Tier allowance). Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS): USD 0.00/month (15,000 standard requests, free within the 1 million requests Free Tier). Amazon EventBridge: USD 0.00/month (3,000 custom events within the Free Tier allowance). Amazon SNS: USD 0.00/month (100 free email alert requests). AWS CloudTrail: USD 0.00/month (administrative Event History for 90 days is 100% free). Total cost: USD 5.14/month, equivalent to USD 61.68/12 months (approximately ~VND 1,540,000 for a full year of operation).
8. Risk Assessment & Mitigation Risk matrix
Web vulnerabilities / data theft: high impact, medium probability. AI giving wrong part specifications: high impact, low probability. Cost spikes due to API spam: medium impact, low probability. Mitigation strategies
Block attacks at the edge with Edge WAF, and verify JWT tokens to prevent viewing other people’s orders (IDOR protection). Strictly constrain the AI prompt: only answer what is in the technical documents and never invent specifications. Set rate limits on API Gateway and configure AWS Budgets cost alerts. Contingency plans
When the bot cannot handle a case, it automatically escalates to a support staff member by email, together with the customer’s information. The entire infrastructure is defined in Terraform files and can be fully rebuilt in another region within 15 minutes in case of an incident. 9. Expected Results Technical improvements: Successfully build a complete Serverless e-commerce system combined with real-time AI RAG, automatically scaling with load without anyone on duty to operate servers. Practical value: Helps motorcycle parts stores reduce advisory staffing costs, lower the rate of customers buying wrong parts, and save as much budget as possible for the company/store owner.

content:
Summary Report: “Navigating the Future of Cloud & AI in Vietnam” The event featured a keynote by Werner Vogels, CTO of Amazon, on lessons from operating large-scale systems and the role of developers in the AI era.
Event Information Event Name: Navigating the Future of Cloud & AI in Vietnam Date & Time: 02/10/2026, 09:00 – 12:00 Venue: Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City Participation Role: Attendee Core Learning: Lessons from operating large-scale systems and the profile of a “Renaissance Developer” Event Objectives Share why Amazon had to build its own core technology when existing solutions could no longer meet its scale Present the principles for operating large systems reliably Address whether developers will be replaced as AI automates coding Point out the qualities developers need to build in order to keep up Speakers Werner Vogels - CTO, Amazon Key Highlights From a multi-million-dollar outage to homegrown core technology When Werner Vogels left Cornell University to join Amazon more than two decades ago, no existing software could meet the company’s scale On a peak shopping day, 12/12, the relational database cluster was overloaded and a latent bug disrupted customer data storage for a day, costing millions of dollars The vendor said Amazon had been using the product beyond its design limits Amazon then re-examined how its databases were used:
Query type Share Characteristics Key-value About 70% Simple lookups, such as fetching a cart by ID Single table About 20% Work on one table, without links Relational About 10% Truly need relational database features Based on this result, Amazon built its own distributed key-value store, the foundation of Dynamo and DynamoDB.
Four pillars of operational excellence Pillar Meaning Measure at P99.9 Median latency hides the experience of the half of users with worse results, so the slowest group must be watched Everything Fails All the Time The architecture must survive the sudden loss of one or two data centers without service disruption GameDays Deliberately disconnect production data centers as a drill, remove manual steps, and automate data sync on recovery Inverting the IT economic model Pay-as-you-go replaces long upfront contracts, so the provider must serve well every day to keep customers Profile of a “Renaissance Developer” Developers remain valuable if they are willing to change. The speaker named five qualities:
Curiosity and continuous learning: never stop exploring new technology Systems thinking: understand how microservices interact at scale, not just one separate module Ownership: AI can generate code, but engineers remain responsible for production bugs, security, and architecture T-shaped expertise: go deep in one field and broadly understand adjacent ones such as UI, business logic, and databases Communication: find the real problem behind hype-driven requests and explain trade-offs, such as the cost gap between 99.99% and 99% uptime AI as a catalyst, humans at the core AI has cut prototyping time from weeks to hours AI was compared to a natural-language compiler that is not fully precise, so its output needs human review for security, edge cases, and efficiency AI handles repetitive work well, while judgment, creativity, empathy, and professional pride still belong to humans A quote shared in the talk “We’ve always done it this way” is the most dangerous phrase, according to Grace Hopper’s warning repeated by the speaker.
Key Takeaways Architecture Mindset Analyze how data is really accessed before choosing a database At very large scale, depending on existing solutions can become an operational risk Operations Mindset Design with the assumption that every component can fail Recovery can only be trusted once it has been rehearsed Averages and medians are not enough to judge user experience Career Mindset Use AI to work faster but stay responsible for the result Build both technical depth and communication skills Applying to Work Choose databases by query pattern, preferring DynamoDB for key-value lookups Track latency by percentile in CloudWatch instead of looking only at the average Design for failure with retries, Dead Letter Queues, and alarms Run small-scale failure drills in a lab environment Review AI-generated code carefully, especially for security and edge cases Event Experience Attending Navigating the Future of Cloud & AI in Vietnam gave me a clearer view of what lies behind a large-scale system and the role of engineers when AI is there to help.
Learning from the speaker The story of the database outage showed me that a good architecture decision starts with understanding your own data. The five qualities of a “Renaissance Developer” gave me a clear framework for self-assessment. Perspective on AI I understood that AI changes how we work, but responsibility for security and quality still belongs to engineers. This is close to Information Assurance, the major I am studying. Lessons learned Reliable systems are built by accepting that failures will happen. Continuous learning and systems thinking matter more than only knowing how to use one tool. A way of working should not be kept just because it has always been done that way. Reference: The Invariable Lessons of Tech and Humanity: Key Takeaways from Amazon CTO Werner Vogels – Le Vu Xuan An, AWS Builder Center
Some event photos Event Check-in Verification — Community Workshop
Overall, the event helped me understand that technology changes quickly, but systems thinking, responsibility, and continuous learning remain the foundation of an engineer.

OPENING THE AWS BILL EVERY MONTH AND ASKING “WHY DID COSTS SPIKE?” — WHAT IF AN AGENT FOUND THE ANSWER AUTOMATICALLY? AUTOMATING CLOUD FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT WITH AWS FINOPS AGENT Link to the original post: AWS Study Group VN – Facebook
In many organizations, cloud cost management still operates on a periodic cycle. At the end of the month, the FinOps team opens a dashboard and discovers an abnormal cost spike in a service. They then have to filter data in Cost Explorer, correlate it with infrastructure change history, and ask individual teams who created or modified resources.
This process is time-consuming. More importantly, it is reactive: by the time the root cause is identified, the cost has already been accumulating for days. This raises a key question: does cost investigation really have to wait for monthly review meetings, or can it happen the moment an anomaly appears?
AWS FinOps Agent entered public preview on 09/06/2026. Built on Amazon Bedrock, this frontier agent is designed to answer cost questions, automatically investigate cost anomalies, and execute recurring FinOps workflows. This approach shifts Cloud Financial Management from manual periodic reviews to continuous, event-driven operations.
1. WHAT PROBLEM DOES AWS FINOPS AGENT SOLVE? FinOps (Financial Operations) is a discipline that connects finance, engineering, and business teams. Its goal is to maximize the business value of cloud investments through shared financial accountability and data-driven decision-making.
The challenge is that cost data and operational data often live in separate silos. Cost Anomaly Detection can alert you that spending is rising, but it does not tell you which infrastructure change caused it, who owns the resource, or how to remediate it. That investigation still relies heavily on human effort.
AWS FinOps Agent takes on this exact responsibility. Engineers can ask questions in natural language, such as “Why did our AWS costs increase last month?”. The agent responds based on actual cost and usage data: how much spending changed, which services contributed the most, and which specific usage factors drove the increase.
2. ARCHITECTURE AND CORE COMPONENTS The agent is provisioned inside an AWS account, runs in the US East (N. Virginia) Region, and users interact with it through a chat-based web application.
Amazon Bedrock provides the foundation models for reasoning and investigation planning.
On the data side, the agent integrates several existing AWS services:
AWS Cost Explorer: cost and usage data. AWS Cost Anomaly Detection: emits events when spending anomalies occur. AWS Cost Optimization Hub and AWS Compute Optimizer: recommendations for rightsizing, idle resources, and Savings Plans. AWS CloudTrail: audit logs of who changed what, and when. Notably, the agent does not create a new cost data silo. Instead, it sits above the cost management services the organization already uses and connects them into a unified investigation workflow.
Additionally, teams can upload context files such as account-to-owner mappings, team definitions, tagging conventions, or review cadences. The agent applies this organizational context to its answers and retains memory across sessions.
Results are delivered directly to the tools engineers already use: posting investigation reports to Slack or opening tickets in Jira.
3. HOW DOES COST ANOMALY INVESTIGATION WORK? The agent can be configured to listen for events from Cost Anomaly Detection.
When an alert is triggered, the agent correlates the cost fluctuation against events in AWS CloudTrail. From there, it identifies which infrastructure change led to the spike and compiles an investigation report detailing the likely root cause and the responsible owner.
The report is sent to a Slack channel or created as a Jira ticket, allowing engineering teams to receive actionable insights without manual triage.
Alongside this event-driven model, the agent can also run scheduled workflows defined by users—for example, generating periodic cost reports for finance and engineering teams.
4. ACCESS CONTROL AND SECURITY When an AI agent is granted access to financial and operational data, access control becomes critically important.
The agent accesses data through a customer-managed IAM role. Organizations can restrict which accounts, services, and actions the agent is allowed to use, strictly following the principle of least privilege.
AWS also provides blast-radius controls and rollback mechanisms. Users can define boundaries across dimensions such as accounts, Regions, or maximum financial impact.
All agent activities are logged in AWS CloudTrail within the host account, creating a complete audit trail to verify what the agent accessed and when.
5. GETTING STARTED According to AWS documentation, the setup process consists of five steps:
Sign in to the AWS Management Console, switch to the us-east-1 Region, and open the AWS FinOps Agent console to create your first agent. Configure the IAM role with a single click. This customer-managed role allows the agent to read cost, usage, and operational data. Connect Jira and Slack (optional). Review the agent configuration. Launch the web application to start interacting with the agent. 6. LIMITATIONS TO CONSIDER Although AWS FinOps Agent significantly reduces manual investigation overhead, it is still in preview. Features and scope may change before General Availability (GA).
During the preview period, the agent is only hosted in US East (N. Virginia). Cost data covers all AWS Regions except AWS GovCloud (US) and Regions in China. The service is free during preview but subject to monthly usage limits and service quotas. GA pricing has not yet been announced, so total cost of ownership cannot be fully evaluated yet.
The agent only works with AWS data. Organizations operating in multi-cloud environments will still need additional tools for a consolidated cross-cloud cost view.
Answer quality also depends on input data quality. If resource tagging is inconsistent or owner mappings are outdated, the agent will struggle to pinpoint the exact responsible team.
Finally, the agent does not replace the FinOps team. Root cause conclusions still require human verification before making infrastructure changes or committing to Savings Plans.
CONCLUSION Having a cost dashboard does not automatically mean having cost control. What truly matters is delivering anomaly insights to the right person, at the right time, with a clear enough root cause to take action.
AWS FinOps Agent is a promising approach for organizations with multiple accounts and teams that frequently spend hours investigating cost fluctuations.
However, real-world effectiveness depends on proper IAM permission scoping, tagging hygiene, organizational context, and the eventual GA pricing model.
Cloud cost optimization is not just about cutting resources—it is about closing the gap between the moment a cost anomaly occurs and the moment the team truly understands why.

Event Information Event Name: Enterprise AI on AWS Cloud: From Prototype to Production Date & Time: 14/11/2026, 09:00 – 12:00 Venue: 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City Participation Role: Attendee Core Learning: Production AI architecture: 4 operational pillars and Multi-Agent patterns Program: FPT University Workshop, organized by First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) Format: Workshop with three sessions: moving AI from prototype to production, case studies, and AI in enterprise with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Event Objectives Explain the gap between an academic AI prototype and an enterprise AI system Present the four pillars of production AI (security, scalability, reliability and cost) and how the cloud supports them Learn from real case studies: Cox Automotive, Mobileye and Duolingo Introduce Amazon Bedrock AgentCore as a foundation for running agents in an enterprise Speakers Khang Duong – FCAJ member Phuong Huyen – AI Engineer Fresher, FPT Software Nguyen Lam Anh – AI Engineer, FCAJ Key Highlights Session 1: From Prototype to Production – Secure, Reliable, Scalable Enterprise AI on the Cloud One restaurant, one story
The speaker used a restaurant analogy throughout the session:
Prototype = a home kitchen Enterprise AI = a restaurant chain Cloud = a central kitchen AI in the enterprise
The flow is Data (ingredients) → AI model (the chef) → Feature (the dish) → Users (customers) AI is usually a feature inside a product, for example recommendations, a support chatbot or fraud detection Academic AI vs. enterprise AI
Aspect Academic AI (home kitchen) Enterprise AI (restaurant chain) Goal Accuracy Business value Data Clean, fixed dataset Real, ever-changing data Users A few people Millions of users Operation One-off run 24/7, no downtime More than a model
The model is only “the recipe”. A production system also needs a data pipeline, security, scalability, reliability, monitoring and cost control Elastic scalability: a fixed kitchen wastes capacity when demand is low and fails when demand peaks, while an elastic kitchen follows demand. On AWS, Lambda automatically clones itself, Auto Scaling adds or removes capacity, and a Load Balancer shares the load Reliability: if one oven breaks, a backup is ready. Tools include health checks, retry, failover and alarms Cost efficiency: do not keep everything running when nobody is there. Use pay-per-use, right-sizing and caching Elastic Scaling on AWS
AWS services absorb fluctuating AI workloads automatically.
Service Role AWS Lambda Serverless; scales per request and down to zero when idle Auto Scaling Groups Adds or removes EC2 inference instances based on CloudWatch metrics (CPU, GPU memory, queue depth) ALB/NLB Distributes traffic and runs health checks to isolate failed nodes The role of the cloud
Built-in security, scaling on demand, backup zones for reliability and pay-as-you-go pricing The shared responsibility is clear: AWS manages the infrastructure, and customers manage their data and usage Session 2: From Prototype to Production – Case Study Cox Automotive
29,000+ employees on five continents, 2.3 billion online interactions a year (first-party data) and 57 agentic AI opportunities identified Business areas: car buying and selling, auctions, dealer software and fleet services Key question: “How do you build automated AI solutions that users will trust?” Approach: standardize the foundation first with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore AgentCore Runtime: one runtime for all agents, covering deployment, monitoring, error handling and security patterns; it runs Strands multi-agent systems AgentCore Identity: granular, role-based permissions for each agent Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: screens inputs and outputs, with multi-layered security and prompt hardening AgentCore Memory: context across sessions and customer preferences AgentCore Observability: logs every interaction so multi-step reasoning can be debugged Mobileye
Skilled engineers were spending their time answering status tickets: 66% of support tickets were routine status inquiries, and each ticket took about 15 clicks across several backend systems Context: 230M+ EyeQ chips deployed, with a data pipeline ingesting thousands of drive-recording sessions every day Why rule-based automation was not enough: scripts and decision trees handle predictable queries but not the variety of real requests Hybrid design where on-premises tickets meet a cloud agent: On-premises: a local orchestrator pulls tickets and posts replies; the ticket system is not reachable from AWS AWS AgentCore: the support agent runs on AgentCore Runtime, and credentials stay in Secrets Manager and are never exposed Mobileye services: a data pipeline MCP server provides live status, logs and errors, and an LLM gateway serves Claude with quota management AgentCore Observability traces each request through the MCP tool calls to the reply There is no inbound path into the on-premises network, and live data reaches the model at inference time through MCP Session 3: AI in Enterprise (Part 2) – Enterprise Challenges and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Today’s journey
Duolingo case study: why shared AI platforms matter Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Strands, Runtime and the AgentCore map Key Takeaways Production Mindset A working prototype only proves that an idea is possible. Production has to prove that it keeps working for many people, every day, at a cost the company can accept The model is the part people notice, but data, security, monitoring and cost control decide whether the system survives 4 Pillars of Production AI Security, Reliability, Scalability, and Cost Optimization form the foundation of a production AI system.
Security: KMS encryption, IAM, VPC Endpoints, and Bedrock Guardrails to prevent data leakage and prompt injection. Reliability: Multi-AZ deployment, exponential backoff retries, and failover. Scalability: Elastic compute that absorbs traffic spikes without bottlenecks. Cost: Right-sizing, serverless pricing, and model routing (a small model for simple queries, a large model for complex ones). Token Economics and Inference Token count drives both latency and cost.
Input and output tokens directly affect response time and the cloud bill. Practical levers include prompt optimization, context compression, and prompt caching. Training runs in periodic batches on GPU/Trainium clusters. Inference runs 24/7 and needs millisecond-to-second latency. Enterprise Agents Building the shared foundation first (runtime, identity, guardrails, memory, observability) keeps each new agent from solving the same problems again The Mobileye case shows that a company does not have to open its internal network to benefit from cloud agents With MCP, an agent can look up live data when it answers instead of relying only on what the model already knows Multi-Agent Architecture Patterns Split complex workflows across specialized agents when a single LLM is not enough.
Pattern Mechanism Typical Use Case Routing / Supervisor A central agent routes each query to the right specialist Multi-service customer support Sequential Each agent’s output becomes the next agent’s input Loan application review Parallel Agents run independent subtasks at once; a synthesizer merges the results Analysis across multiple data sources Evaluator–Optimizer One agent generates output, another critiques it, and the loop repeats until it meets the quality bar Code generation, legal drafting Applying to Work Evaluate my internship projects against the 4 pillars. Apply prompt caching and context compression to control Amazon Bedrock cost and latency. Use the Supervisor and Evaluator–Optimizer patterns for multi-step data processing and automated testing. Use Lambda and Auto Scaling Groups for inference that scales with traffic. Think beyond the model in my AI projects by planning the data pipeline, monitoring and cost from the start Add reliability basics such as health checks, retries and alarms Try Amazon Bedrock AgentCore components (Runtime, Identity, Memory, Observability) for a small agent project Keep credentials in Secrets Manager and add guardrails to filter inputs and outputs Event Experience What I liked most about Enterprise AI on AWS Cloud: From Prototype to Production was that it made me think about a simple question: why do so many good demos struggle once real people use them?
Learning from speakers The kitchen comparison was easy to picture, and I can use it myself to explain cloud and AI to people outside the field. Hearing an AI engineer who started recently at FPT Software speak made this path feel closer to students like me. Real case studies Cox Automotive showed me that trust in agents comes from permissions, guardrails and logs, not from the model alone. Mobileye reminded me that a useful AI project can begin with a small, repetitive task such as answering status tickets. Networking and discussions Exchanging ideas with FCAJ members, students and engineers let me compare how different people approach the same AI problem. Lessons learned I should define how a system will be monitored and protected before adding more features to it. From a security point of view, every agent needs its own identity and only the permissions it really uses. Starting small on a solid foundation is safer than building many agents that each work in a different way. Some event photos Event Check-in Verification — From Prototype to Production Workshop
After the workshop, I see a prototype as the beginning of the work: the harder part is making it safe, stable and affordable enough for people to rely on.

title: Blog 3
content:
RANSOMWARE DELETES THE BACKUPS TOO - HOW DO YOU KEEP A COPY NOBODY CAN DELETE? Link to the original post: AWS Study Group VN – Facebook
The question is this: if an attacker already has admin rights, is there a backup that even the admin cannot delete? AWS Backup Vault Lock was designed to answer exactly that.
1. WHY DO YOU STILL LOSE DATA WHEN YOU HAVE BACKUPS? Modern ransomware does not encrypt as soon as it gets in. Attackers usually stay hidden, escalate privileges, and cut off the victim’s way back before triggering encryption. MITRE ATT&CK describes this step as technique T1490 (Inhibit System Recovery), alongside T1485 (Data Destruction) and T1486 (Data Encrypted for Impact).
In the cloud, this scenario is simpler than many people think. If backups live in the same account as the workload, a single access key with admin rights is enough to delete snapshots, delete recovery points, and delete the backup vault itself with a few API calls.
The core problem is that the right to delete backups and the right to administer the system belong to the same identity. When that identity is compromised, the original data and its copies are lost together. A ransomware-resistant backup strategy therefore has to meet three requirements: the copy cannot be deleted or altered (immutable), it sits apart from the production environment (isolated), and it has been checked as clean before restore (verified).
2. ARCHITECTURE AND MAIN COMPONENTS The architecture uses three accounts in the same AWS Organization: a workload account running production, a backup account managed by the data protection team, and a recovery account used only during an incident. The diagram below numbers the six steps of this flow.
Each service has its own role:
AWS Organizations: applies service control policies (SCPs) and backup policies from the management account to every member account. AWS Backup: runs tag-based backup plans and creates recovery points for Amazon EC2, Amazon EBS, Amazon RDS, and Amazon S3. Backup vault with Vault Lock: holds the first copy inside the workload account, where nobody can delete it before the retention period ends. Logically air-gapped vault: holds the second copy in the backup account, locked automatically in compliance mode and encrypted by default with an AWS owned key. Amazon GuardDuty Malware Protection for AWS Backup: scans recovery points for malware after each backup. Amazon EventBridge and Amazon SNS: turn scan results into alerts for the security team. AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) and Multi-party approval: share the vault with the recovery account when a restore is needed. What stands out is that this architecture does not rely on a single layer of protection. Vault Lock prevents deletion, a separate account stops privileges from spreading, SCPs block destructive actions at the organization level, and GuardDuty answers which backup is still clean. Each layer is an independent boundary, so an attacker who gets past one is still stopped by another.
3. HOW DOES VAULT LOCK WORK? AWS Backup Vault Lock applies the WORM (write once, read many) model to a backup vault. Once the vault is locked, AWS Backup rejects every request to delete a recovery point or change its lifecycle, even when the request comes from the root user.
Vault Lock has two modes. In governance mode, anyone with sufficient IAM permissions can still remove the lock, which makes it suitable for testing and for guarding against accidental deletion. In compliance mode, once the waiting period has passed, nobody can change or remove the lock, including the account owner and AWS itself.
That waiting period is called grace time, with a minimum of 3 days (72 hours). During it, the lock can still be modified or deleted. It is the last chance to catch a misconfiguration, because after that point everything becomes immutable.
Vault Lock also lets you set a minimum and maximum retention period. Backup or copy jobs whose retention falls outside that range fail. This stops an attacker from working around the lock by creating backups that live for one day and waiting for them to expire.
The following example creates a compliance mode lock with a 3-day grace time and retention between 7 and 35 days:
aws backup put-backup-vault-lock-configuration \ --backup-vault-name prod-vault \ --changeable-for-days 3 \ --min-retention-days 7 \ --max-retention-days 35 If you omit the --changeable-for-days parameter, the lock is created in governance mode.
4. ISOLATING BACKUPS AND DETECTING MALWARE BEFORE RESTORE Immutability is only half the answer. If the only copy still sits in the compromised account, the attacker cannot delete it but can still obstruct recovery.
Recovery points are therefore copied to a logically air-gapped vault in the backup account. This type of vault is locked automatically with Vault Lock in compliance mode, is encrypted by default with an AWS owned key, and requires a minimum retention of 7 days. It can be shared through AWS RAM so another account can restore from it directly, without copying the data back.
At the organization level, SCPs block dangerous actions such as backup:DeleteRecoveryPoint, backup:DeleteBackupVault, and backup:UpdateRecoveryPointLifecycle. SCPs apply even to admins of member accounts, so credentials stolen in production are not enough to destroy the backups.
The remaining question is which backup is still clean. Ransomware can stay hidden for weeks, so the most recent backup may not be usable. Amazon GuardDuty Malware Protection for AWS Backup, launched on 19/11/2025, scans Amazon EC2, Amazon EBS, and Amazon S3 recovery points after each backup. The result is either NO_THREATS_FOUND or THREATS_FOUND, and it is also published as an event on Amazon EventBridge so alerts can be sent through Amazon SNS.
When recovery is needed, the operations team picks the most recent clean recovery point and restores it into the recovery account. Since 17/06/2025, logically air-gapped vaults also support Multi-party approval: a group of trusted people must approve together before the vault is shared, even when the account that owns the vault is no longer accessible.
5. GETTING STARTED The architecture can be rolled out in six steps:
Create a dedicated backup account in AWS Organizations and enable cross-account backup from the management account. Create a backup vault in the workload account and enable Vault Lock. Try governance mode first, then create the compliance mode lock. Create a logically air-gapped vault in the backup account, then add it as a copy destination in the backup plan. Attach SCPs that block backup deletion and modification actions to the member accounts. Enable malware scanning in the backup plan, create an EventBridge rule for THREATS_FOUND results, and send them to the security team’s SNS topic. Share the vault with the recovery account through AWS RAM and run restore testing on a schedule. 6. LIMITATIONS TO CONSIDER Compliance mode cannot be undone. If retention is set too long, the organization pays for storage until it expires. Recovery points with “Always” retention are kept forever once grace time ends. Vault Lock only controls operations that go through AWS Backup. According to the AWS documentation, direct EC2 API calls such as ec2:ModifySnapshotAttribute can still share a snapshot externally, and ec2:DisableImage can block a restore. These actions need to be blocked separately with IAM policies or SCPs. The lock does not protect a closed account. If the account is not reopened within 90 days, AWS deletes the vault contents even with Vault Lock in place. Immutable does not mean clean. GuardDuty only reports scan results; it does not delete or block infected recovery points, and scanning is billed under GuardDuty. Incremental scans do not yet support EC2 recovery points stored in a logically air-gapped vault. It does not stop data theft. In double extortion, attackers threaten to publish the data rather than only encrypting it, and backups do not address that risk. Cost and coverage. Keeping two copies increases storage cost, and logically air-gapped vaults do not yet support every resource type or every Region. A backup that has never been test-restored cannot be considered trustworthy. 7. CONCLUSION Having backups does not guarantee you can recover. What matters is that a copy exists beyond the reach of the very identities that can be compromised.
AWS Backup Vault Lock, combined with a logically air-gapped vault, SCPs, and GuardDuty Malware Protection, is an approach worth considering for organizations running critical workloads on AWS, especially in finance, securities, and e-commerce.
Its real-world effectiveness, however, depends on how accounts are separated, how retention is designed, and how regularly restores are rehearsed.
Fighting ransomware is not only about keeping attackers out. It is also about making sure that when every other layer of defense fails, the organization still has a clean copy to go back to.
References:
AWS Backup Developer Guide – AWS Backup Vault Lock AWS Backup Developer Guide – Logically air-gapped vault AWS Storage Blog – Securing backup data against modern threats with AWS Backup

List of technical blog posts written during the internship program.
Blog 1 - Amazon Inspector Security is often thought of mainly as configuring IAM permissions and closing unnecessary ports. However, a server can be well-configured and still be compromised simply because the software inside remains unpatched. A single outdated library or an unpatched OS package is enough to give attackers a way in.

Looked at the “Allow external principals” option and how to limit sharing to the organization only 25/09/2026 25/09/2026 AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) Console AWS RAM User Guide Week 3 Achievements: Resource Shares (AWS RAM): Sharing regional resources (VPC subnets, Transit Gateways, Route 53 rules) across accounts using resources, principals, and managed permissions Organizations vs. External Sharing: Seamless invitation-free sharing inside AWS Organizations/OUs vs. explicit invitation acceptance for external accounts CLI & Boundary Security: Understanding how the aws ram CLI manages shares and how to restrict external sharing with ram:RequestedAllowsExternalPrincipals SCP conditions AWS RAM solves resource duplication in multi-account setups by letting one owner account share infrastructure directly with other accounts. Unlike cross-account IAM roles—where a user switches identity to access another account—RAM makes the shared resource (such as a VPC subnet) appear natively inside the recipient account so teams can launch EC2 instances into it while the owner account retains full control over the subnet itself.
Key takeaways:
Native Resource Sharing: Shared resources can be used directly by recipient accounts without duplicating infrastructure or managing extra IAM users. Owner Control Preserved: Recipient accounts can use a shared resource within managed permissions, but only the owner account can modify or delete it. Organization Guardrails: Disabling external principals and enforcing SCP conditions prevents accidental resource sharing outside the organization.

Gave a Lambda function permission to read only one secret and called it from code instead of hard-coding the value 02/10/2026 02/10/2026 Amazon Cognito Developer Guide AWS Secrets Manager User Guide Week 4 Achievements: Cognito User Pools & Tokens: Managing sign-up/sign-in, MFA, and JWT tokens (ID, Access, and Refresh tokens) to authenticate application users Identity Pools & API Security: Exchanging valid logins for temporary AWS credentials and securing API Gateway endpoints with Cognito Authorizers AWS Secrets Manager: Encrypting database credentials and API keys with KMS, automating secret rotation, and restricting GetSecretValue to specific ARNs This week focused on two essentials of application security: verifying user identity with Amazon Cognito and eliminating hard-coded credentials with AWS Secrets Manager. Testing both services clarified that User Pools handle authentication (“who are you?” via JWT tokens), Identity Pools handle AWS authorization (“what can you access?” via temporary IAM credentials), and Secrets Manager lets backend functions fetch encrypted credentials at runtime instead of storing secrets in source code.
Key takeaways:
Authentication vs. Authorization: User Pools issue tokens for login and API Gateway checks, while Identity Pools map users to temporary IAM roles. Zero Hard-Coded Secrets: Applications retrieve credentials dynamically from Secrets Manager so keys can be updated or rotated in one place without changing code. Scoped Secret Access: Each Lambda function should only have secretsmanager:GetSecretValue permission for the single secret ARN it requires, with every read audited in CloudTrail.

title: Cleanup Resources
content:
After completing the workshop and verifying all system flows, we should clean up all provisioned AWS resources to avoid unexpected ongoing charges.
Step 1: Empty S3 Buckets AWS does not allow deleting non-empty S3 buckets. Empty all 3 S3 buckets in the lab environment before running terraform destroy:
# 1. Empty S3 Hosting Bucket (Frontend Static Assets) aws s3 rm s3://<s3_hosting_bucket_name> --recursive # 2. Empty S3 Product Images Bucket aws s3 rm s3://<s3_product_images_bucket_name> --recursive # 3. Empty S3 Chatbot Knowledge Base Bucket (Vector JSON) aws s3 rm s3://<chatbot_kb_bucket_name> --recursive Note (Delete All Versions): For S3 buckets with Versioning enabled (such as phutungxemay-product-images-lab-2026), aws s3 rm only adds delete markers without permanently removing previous object versions. Run the following Python command to purge all versions and delete markers before running terraform destroy:
python -c "import boto3; boto3.resource('s3').Bucket('<s3_product_images_bucket_name>').object_versions.delete()" (Alternatively, open AWS Console -> S3 -> select the bucket -> click Empty -> type permanently delete.)
Step 2: Destroy Infrastructure via Terraform Open Terminal / PowerShell, navigate to the terraform directory, and run:
cd <project-path>/phutungxemay-platform/terraform terraform destroy Terraform will display the full list of resources scheduled for deletion (CloudFront, REST & WebSocket API Gateways, 13 Lambda Functions, 6 DynamoDB Tables, Cognito User Pool, EventBridge, SQS, SNS, CloudWatch Dashboard/Alarms, Secrets Manager, IAM Roles, etc.). Type yes and press Enter to confirm. Wait approximately 3 – 5 minutes for deletion to complete (disabling and deleting the CloudFront distribution takes the longest). Expected Result:
Step 3: Delete Remaining CloudWatch Log Groups CloudWatch Log Groups automatically generated by Lambda executions at runtime are not removed by terraform destroy. To keep the account clean:
Open AWS Console -> CloudWatch -> Log groups. Filter by the environment suffix (e.g., -Lab). Select all project log groups (e.g., /aws/lambda/NextjsServerHandler-Lab, /aws/lambda/ChatOrchestratorHandler-Lab, etc.). Click Actions -> Delete log group(s) -> Confirm deletion. Step 4: Remove Deployment IAM User & Policy (Optional) If we no longer need the terraform-deployer account:
Open AWS Console -> IAM -> Users -> Select terraform-deployer -> Click Delete (this also removes its Access Keys).
Navigate to Policies -> Search for MotorcycleEcommerceTerraformPolicy -> Click Delete.

title: Workshop
content:
Building a Serverless E-Commerce Platform & Full-Duplex AI RAG Chatbot on AWS Overview In this workshop, we will build and deploy an end-to-end 100% Serverless Motorcycle Spare Parts E-Commerce Platform integrated with a Real-Time Full-Duplex AI RAG Chatbot on AWS in the ap-southeast-1 (Singapore) region.
The entire cloud infrastructure is automated via Terraform (Infrastructure as Code) following Least Privilege security principles and Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) best practices.
Throughout this lab, we will implement three core modern cloud pillars on AWS:
Serverless Web & Microservices: Deliver a Next.js SSR storefront via Amazon CloudFront (+ Edge WAF), Amazon S3, and AWS Lambda; backed by Amazon Cognito, API Gateway (REST API), and Amazon DynamoDB. Event-Driven Architecture (EDA): Decouple asynchronous order fulfillment workflows using Amazon EventBridge and Amazon SQS (Inventory Worker for stock deduction, Shipping Worker integrated with GHN Sandbox, and Notification Worker sending emails via Gmail SMTP). Full-Duplex AI RAG Chatbot & CDC: Build a real-time two-way chat channel using API Gateway WebSocket with a Lambda Authorizer verifying Cognito JWTs, in-memory vector search on Amazon S3 powered by Google Gemini 2.0 Flash, and automated knowledge sync via DynamoDB Streams. Updated the packages on the instance and checked that the findings were closed. Compared GuardDuty and Inspector side by side 09/10/2026 09/10/2026 Amazon GuardDuty User Guide Amazon Inspector User Guide Week 5 Achievements: Amazon GuardDuty: Agentless threat detection across CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs (plus optional S3, EKS, RDS, and Lambda protection) Alerting & Signal Tuning: Routing high-severity findings to email via EventBridge + SNS and filtering noise with suppression rules / trusted IP lists Amazon Inspector: Automated CVE and network exposure scanning across EC2, ECR images, and Lambda functions with risk-based prioritization GuardDuty vs. Inspector: GuardDuty detects active attacks happening now; Inspector identifies software weaknesses before they are exploited While both services strengthen cloud security, they solve two different sides of the problem: Inspector checks whether the door is unlocked, and GuardDuty warns when someone is trying to break in. Scanning an outdated EC2 instance with Inspector showed me how quickly unpatched packages accumulate CVEs—and watching those findings close automatically after updating the packages made continuous vulnerability scanning and automated EventBridge alerting feel practical.
Key takeaways:
Proactive vs. Reactive Detection: Inspector finds software CVEs before an attack occurs, while GuardDuty spots live threats like SSH brute-force or port probing in real time. Zero-Agent Visibility: GuardDuty analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs directly without requiring manual log setup. Automated Alerting: Pairing GuardDuty and Inspector with EventBridge and SNS ensures critical findings reach engineers immediately without manual console checks.

EC2 provides a full virtual machine where I control the OS and networking—but because it bills for every hour the server is running, unused instances must be stopped. Lightsail trades deep customization for speed and a fixed monthly bundle, while Lambda removes server management entirely so code only exists and costs money when triggered by an event such as an API Gateway request.
Key takeaways:
Control vs. Convenience: Use EC2 when deep OS/network customization is required, and Lightsail when launching small apps or websites quickly. Pay-for-Uptime vs. Pay-per-Execution: EC2 charges while running even if idle, whereas Lambda bills strictly for request count and execution duration. Compute Security: Restrict EC2 SSH access to specific IPs in Security Groups, and grant Lambda functions minimal IAM Execution Roles.

Managed API Front Door: API Gateway handles public request routing and stages without exposing backend compute directly.

Learned why it is better to disable a key or schedule deletion with a waiting period than to delete it right away 27/11/2026 27/11/2026 AWS KMS Documentation AWS CloudHSM Documentation Week 12 Achievements: AWS KMS: KMS is a managed service for creating and controlling encryption keys. The keys stay inside KMS and are used to encrypt data in services like S3, EBS, RDS and Secrets Manager Key Types: AWS owned and AWS managed keys are handled by AWS. Customer managed keys give me control over the policy, rotation and deletion Envelope Encryption: Instead of sending large data to KMS, a small data key encrypts the data, and the KMS key encrypts that data key Key Security: Use key policies with least privilege, turn on automatic rotation, check key usage in CloudTrail, and use the waiting period before deleting a key AWS CloudHSM: CloudHSM is a dedicated, single-tenant hardware device in my VPC. I manage the keys and users myself, and AWS cannot see the keys KMS vs. CloudHSM: KMS is easier and cheaper for most cases. CloudHSM is for strict compliance rules or when a company needs full control of the hardware For the last week, I studied something that sits under almost everything I learned before: encryption keys. S3, EBS, RDS and Secrets Manager all depend on them, but until now I had never looked at where the keys actually come from.
KMS turned out to be simpler than I expected. I create a key, decide who can use it, and AWS takes care of keeping it safe. Envelope encryption was the part that took me longest. Thinking of it as “a key inside a locked box” made it click: the data key opens the data, and the KMS key opens the box holding the data key.
CloudHSM felt like the opposite. It gives more control, but I also get more responsibility. If I lose the HSM credentials, nobody can recover the keys for me, not even AWS. That made it clear to me why most projects use KMS, and why CloudHSM is mainly for companies with strict security rules.
Key points learned:
What KMS is and the three types of keys Encrypting S3 and EBS with a customer managed key The basic idea of envelope encryption Protecting keys with key policies, rotation and CloudTrail logs What CloudHSM is and how it is different from KMS Choosing between KMS and CloudHSM based on control, cost and compliance
